warmupTypes.type: General training warm-up (RAMP-style: raise, activate/mobilize, potentiate)

findings.finding: Most controlled studies find a warm-up improves the performance that follows it, and very few find harm.
findings.effect: Performance improved on 79% of the measures examined

findings.finding: The recommended shape is light aerobic work first, then large-range dynamic stretching, then sport-specific dynamic activity.
findings.dose: submaximal raise phase then dynamic and specific phases
findings.effect: Minimizes stretch-related losses and supports power output

findings.finding: Much of a warm-up's benefit comes from raising muscle temperature; a short task-specific burst at the end can add a further boost, and different combinations of intensity, duration and rest can reach the same result.
findings.dose: moderate intensity, followed by a short recovery
findings.effect: Raised muscle temperature and metabolic readiness

findings.finding: A RAMP warm-up (raise, activate, mobilize, potentiate) improved 30-m sprint and jump compared with no warm-up and with static stretching in older adolescent and young adult soccer players.
findings.effect: Moderate improvements in sprint and vertical jump (d about 0.4-0.5)

findings.finding: After a RAMP warm-up, adolescent volleyball players reacted faster to light signals than before it.
Short static stretches inside a full dynamic warm-up neither helped nor hurt sprint, jump or change-of-direction, even though athletes believed stretching helped.
findings.dose: short holds within a full warm-up

findings.finding: Static stretching used as the only warm-up activity causes small losses in strength and explosive performance; losses are smallest when total hold time per muscle is 45 s or less.
findings.dose: keep holds short (45 s or less total per muscle)
findings.effect: About -5% strength, -2% explosive performance when used alone

findings.finding: A newer multilevel meta-analysis found strength loss mainly with holds of 60 s or more per bout and no general harm to athletic performance, so short static stretches do not need to be banned from a warm-up.
findings.effect: Isolated strength loss at long holds; no loss in jump or sprint

findings.finding: Stretching or foam rolling gave no better short-term flexibility than other warm-up activities, so a warm-up does not need dedicated stretching to gain range of motion.

Doing a dynamic warm-up daily over weeks gave lasting gains in power, strength, agility and endurance in wrestlers, and a 10-minute dynamic warm-up improved hamstring flexibility and eccentric quadriceps strength, where static warm-ups did not.
findings.effect: 4% broad jump, 11% quadriceps peak torque over 4 weeks

findings.finding: Warming up also offsets the morning dip in short maximal performance; a longer, more specific warm-up made morning performance match evening performance in young basketball players.
A longer warm-up is not always better: a 15-min cycling warm-up gave no jump benefit over 5 min and lowered power when athletes were fasting.
findings.effect: Longer warm-up added fatigue in a fasted state

findings.finding: Competitive sprinters typically use a three-phase warm-up of about 40 minutes: easy jogging, dynamic or ballistic stretching, then sprint drills and accelerations at the end.
findings.effect: Describes current practice, not an outcome

findings.finding: Adding a heavy or explosive conditioning activity to a warm-up gives a moderate sprint benefit on average, larger in stronger and more experienced athletes.
findings.dose: varies; stronger athletes respond to shorter rest
findings.effect: Moderate effect on sprint (about ES 0.5), small for jumps and throws

findings.finding: For squat-based potentiation, sprint gains appear when the rest after the heavy set is about 4-8 minutes.
findings.effect: Faster 10-m and 30-m sprints, mainly in athletes and ball-sport players

findings.finding: A potentiation effect typically appears 4-9 minutes after the conditioning activity, after an initial period of fatigue; loads of 60% 1RM or more work best for weights.
findings.effect: Short-term enhancement of sprint and jump

findings.finding: A single resisted sprint with about 10% of body mass, followed by several minutes of rest, made later sprints faster in elite female and male college sprinters; 5% and 15% loads were less effective.
findings.dose: 1 sprint at 10% body mass, about 8 min rest
findings.effect: Up to about 4% faster flying 20 m; faster 0-60 m

findings.finding: Different potentiating activities (squats, plyometrics, isometrics) each sped up 20-m sprints, but at different best times after the activity.
findings.effect: Faster 20-m sprints at specific time points

findings.finding: One cluster set of 3 heavy squats with 30-s rest between reps sped up 20-m sprints at 10 minutes in college soccer players.
findings.dose: 3 reps, 30 s between reps, 10 min before

findings.finding: Not every potentiation add-on helps: loaded jump squats did not speed up sprints in college track athletes, and drop jumps did not change sprint times in top-level sprinters.
findings.effect: No average sprint benefit; individual responses varied

findings.finding: A recent meta-analysis found adding potentiation to a general warm-up reliably improves jumping but shows no clear sprint benefit on pooled evidence.
findings.effect: Jump improved; sprint effect not significant

findings.finding: In adolescent boys and girls, 40-s static stretches slowed 20-m sprints by 2.5%, while dynamic stretching did not slow sprinting.
findings.effect: Static stretching hurt sprint; dynamic was neutral

findings.finding: Adding a leg-press potentiation set or mental rehearsal of sprints to a standard warm-up improved agility and repeated-sprint ability.
findings.effect: Better agility and repeated sprints; potentiation also improved 20-m sprint

findings.finding: Low-intensity preparation does not appear to harm landing mechanics: adding static stretching or glute resistance exercises to a dynamic warm-up did not meaningfully change landing kinematics.
A general warm-up improved knee position sense and jump height in sprinters, while a hard plyometric bout afterwards worsened both, with the loss still present 5 minutes later.
findings.dose: warm-up before, not instead of, hard plyometrics
findings.effect: Warm-up helped; fatiguing plyometrics hurt jump and joint sense

findings.finding: In youth soccer players, a warm-up built on stretching (static, dynamic, ballistic or PNF) gave no better jump, sprint or kicking than a standard warm-up.
exercises: static, dynamic, ballistic and PNF stretching

findings.finding: Neuromuscular training (balance, plyometrics, strength) done as the warm-up improved fitness and self-confidence in pubertal soccer players, where stretching-based warm-ups did not.
findings.effect: Large gains in jump, sprint, change of direction and well-being

findings.finding: Short, high-intensity forward-backward hurdle jumps after the warm-up improved sprint and change-of-direction in 12-year-old volleyball players more than low-intensity side-to-side hops.
findings.dose: 3 sets of 6, 2 min rest before testing
findings.effect: Better sprint and COD after the high-intensity version

findings.finding: Rest after a potentiating activity matters for jumps: under about 3-4 minutes the jump is worse, roughly 4-12 minutes is best, and benefits fade after that.
exercises: heavy squats or similar conditioning activity
findings.effect: Higher countermovement jump in the middle window

findings.finding: A 12-week injury-prevention warm-up changed how adolescent female football and handball players pre-activated their thigh muscles before landing during cuts, a pattern thought to protect the ACL.
findings.effect: 43% between-group difference in hamstring vs quadriceps pre-activation; no change in valgus angle

findings.finding: ACL-focused programmes that include plyometrics reduce ACL injuries more than warm-ups without plyometrics, and landing stabilization (jump or hop and hold) is a recommended core component.
Neuromuscular warm-ups improve change-of-direction performance and knee strength compared with regular or dynamic warm-ups; the number of sets moderated the effect.
findings.dose: regular use; more sets gave more benefit
findings.effect: Moderate COD improvement (g about 0.46) and knee strength (g about 0.72)

findings.finding: A 10-minute dynamic warm-up improved a T-shuttle agility run and power tests compared with static stretching or no warm-up in young adults.
Youth sub-elite soccer players using the FIFA 11+ or a modified version over a season improved agility and dribbling speed, with the modified version improving most.
Body-weight alternate-leg bounding improved change-of-direction in women's team-sport players, but only after 8-12 minutes of recovery.
Adding a weighted vest to a badminton warm-up gave small, individual COD effects with no group benefit, so it should be trialled per athlete.
Heavy back squats before testing improved jumps but not the T-test or short sprints in collegiate players.
Equipment-free neuromuscular warm-ups that include agility drills and landing technique reduce lower-limb injuries when used for more than three months.
findings.effect: Large reductions in ACL and knee injuries in some programmes

findings.finding: A shoulder warm-up programme (internal rotation range, external rotation and scapular strength, kinetic chain and thoracic mobility) done as part of the handball warm-up reduced shoulder problems in elite players.
findings.dose: 3 times a week, within the warm-up

findings.finding: In adolescent elite handball players aged 15-19, a Shoulder Control programme lowered shoulder injury risk compared with usual training.
findings.effect: Lower shoulder injury rate; about 1 injury prevented per 9 players

findings.finding: A warm-up of stretching, dynamic mobility and balance exercises halved shoulder and elbow throwing injuries in 9-11-year-old baseball players and improved hip and shoulder range.
findings.effect: Injury rate 1.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 exposures; ball speed tended to rise

findings.finding: External rotation strength training was not inferior to sleeper stretching for preventing arm injuries in high school pitchers, and the strength group had fewer injuries.
A volleyball warm-up shoulder programme used twice a week reduced total injuries and their severity; compliance needs shorter content.
findings.dose: start of practice, twice a week
findings.effect: Fewer and less severe injuries; significant shoulder reduction in men

findings.finding: Across overhead sports, shoulder programmes with strength, stability and sport-specific exercises cut shoulder injuries by about half, but overall evidence is limited and of low certainty.
findings.effect: About 51% fewer shoulder injuries (very low certainty)

findings.finding: The Thrower's Ten band and dumbbell routine improved shoulder stability and flexibility in teen water polo players and is consistently linked to better rotator cuff strength and range.
exercises: Thrower's Ten band and dumbbell exercises
findings.dose: 2 x 10 reps, 3 times weekly for 10 weeks
findings.effect: Better closed-chain stability and rotation range

findings.finding: Pitching 40 hard pitches reduced shoulder rotation range in professional pitchers; a short stretching and calisthenics drill restored it.
findings.effect: Rotation range returned to pre-pitching levels

findings.finding: Weighted or light balls in the warm-up did not change later throwing velocity, and adding isometric or plyometric work to a handball warm-up did not raise throwing speed over a running warm-up.

For hitting, warm-up swings with a standard-weight bat are best supported; on-deck devices from 22 to 96 oz did not change bat speed, while a high-intensity isometric swing hold raised bat speed about 5% at 6 minutes in softball players.
findings.effect: Device weight did not matter; isometric added about 5%

findings.finding: For tennis serves, low-volume flywheel internal-rotation sets raised serve speed 3-6 minutes later without losing accuracy.

Swimmers should warm up about 1000-1500 m with a brief approach to race pace, then rest 8-20 minutes; extras in the transition period (heated jackets, dryland exercises, inspiratory muscle warm-up) can add small gains, but upper-body potentiation often hurts.
Ramping snatch warm-up sets up in smaller 10% steps produced more force and muscle activation in the second pull than 15% steps or a self-chosen ramp.
A movement-specific warm-up of the lift itself raised high-pull power more than cycling or vibration warm-ups that raised muscle temperature.
findings.effect: Specific warm-up gave the largest power gain

findings.finding: Clean and jerk ramp sets (30-80% 1RM) raised both jump and bench-throw height 4-12 minutes later.
findings.dose: 2 min between sets, test 4-12 min after

findings.finding: Power cleans at 90% 1RM gave larger sprint gains than back squats 7 minutes later in elite junior rugby players.
Heavier specific warm-up sets before training (for example at 80% of the training load) gave higher bar velocity in squats than a few light reps.
exercises: specific warm-up sets at 40% or 80% of training load
findings.effect: Higher squat velocity; few light reps were not enough

findings.finding: An extra warm-up set only slightly improved velocity-based 1RM estimates.

A 10-minute stretching routine improved balance in some barbell lifts more than a general 10-minute warm-up, but neither helped complex lifts like the overhead squat; foam rolling gave no better squat depth than a dynamic warm-up.
The NSCA position on weightlifting stresses technique and gradual, sequential progression; specific evidence on mobility drills for catch positions is lacking in the sources reviewed here.
findings.effect: Better force production than general training

warmupTypes.type: Joint-focused warm-ups (ankle, knee, hip/groin, hamstring, shoulder, trunk, neck)

findings.finding: Ankle: warm-up programmes with balance work cut ankle injuries in soccer by about 36%, and multicomponent youth programmes by about 26%.
Ankle: neuromuscular training warm-ups lowered ankle sprains in youth soccer and basketball; a 10-minute basketball warm-up reduced ankle and knee injuries by 36% whether or not it was supervised.
Ankle: an 8-minute warm-up with barefoot single-leg balance, plank and calf stretching improved ankle dorsiflexion and balance in young female basketball players.
findings.dose: 8 min, 3 times a week for 10 weeks
findings.effect: Better dorsiflexion range and postural sway

findings.finding: Knee/ACL: prevention programmes halve all ACL injuries and cut non-contact ACL injuries by about two-thirds in females; balance training adds benefit, especially with three or more sessions a week.
findings.dose: 3+ times per week; 20+ min per week

findings.finding: Knee in female team athletes: benefit depends on compliance of at least 75%, sessions over 15 minutes, 2-3 times a week, with agility and running mechanics.
Groin: a single Copenhagen adductor exercise with three progression levels lowered groin problems by 41% in male footballers; broader groin programmes show a non-significant 19% reduction.
findings.dose: 3 times weekly preseason, once weekly in season

findings.finding: Hamstring: programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise roughly halve hamstring injuries across sports.
Hip and core: a hip and core programme done before running reduced overuse injuries in novice runners, while an ankle and foot programme did not.
Neck: a 10-minute isometric neck warm-up raised neck rate of force development and lateral flexion range in adults, suggesting a short neck primer could be added to contact-sport warm-ups.
exercises: isometric neck holds in all directions

findings.finding: Neck: neck strengthening programmes raise neck strength in age-grade and professional rugby players and are linked to fewer concussions in male rugby; a neuromuscular warm-up in rugby is associated with up to 60% fewer concussions.
findings.effect: About 45% fewer concussions in male rugby

findings.finding: Shoulder: see the throwing section; shoulder programmes inside the warm-up reduce shoulder problems in handball and volleyball.

warmupTypes.type: Pre-game vs pre-practice warm-up, re-warm-up, and how fast the effect fades

findings.finding: Warm-up benefits fade quickly: muscle temperature rises and falls about 0.1 C per minute, a 9-minute rest cut jump height about 4%, and a 23-minute rest reduced lay-up scoring 7% in basketball players.

Keep the gap short: team-sport studies recommend a 10-15 minute active warm-up rising from about 50% to 90% of max heart rate, heated clothing soon after, and about 2 minutes of sprints and jumps if the wait exceeds 15 minutes.
findings.dose: 10-15 min warm-up; 2-min re-warm-up for gaps over 15 min

findings.finding: Professional soccer warm-ups often run 25 minutes or more with about 12 minutes between warm-up and kickoff; only about 2.6 minutes are usually available at half-time.
Half-time re-warm-ups help: they kept sprint speed and reduced jump loss in professional soccer, and meta-analysis shows a moderate jump benefit but trivial sprint effect.
A brief heavy re-warm-up (5-rep max leg press) improved jump and repeated sprints after a break, while a 3-minute small-sided game improved skill execution.
Plyometrics and repeated changes of direction 6 minutes after warm-up limited losses in jump and sprint before a match, while eccentric exercise harmed jump.
Non-starting futsal players who did plyometric and change-of-direction drills after the warm-up kept or improved sprint and COD, while resting or easy stretching made them worse.
Heated trousers for substitutes in cold weather led to more high-speed running once they entered the match.

Pre-match warm-ups in elite futsal last about 27 minutes and build intensity mainly through more accelerations and decelerations; changing the order of phases had small effects in professional soccer.
In swimmers from pre-puberty to adulthood, an active re-warm-up during a 20-25 minute transition outperformed passive rest, especially in younger groups.

warmupTypes.type: Short (8-10 min) vs full (15-20 min) warm-ups and adolescent evidence

findings.finding: Coach-led 20-minute neuromuscular warm-ups in urban public high school girls' soccer and basketball cut non-contact lower-limb injuries by about two-thirds, with coaches using the warm-up at 80% of practices.
findings.effect: IRR 0.33 for acute non-contact lower-limb injuries

findings.finding: A 15-minute neuromuscular warm-up done twice a week cut ACL injuries by 64% in adolescent female football players.
The 11+ style comprehensive warm-up in female footballers aged 13-17 lowered severe injuries, overuse injuries and injuries overall.
exercises: running, strength, plyometric and balance exercises

findings.finding: A 10-minute programme can work: the SHRed basketball warm-up reduced ankle and knee injuries in players aged 11-18.
Shorter programmes also showed benefits: an 8-minute combined warm-up improved ankle range and balance in young female players.
Longer sessions and higher frequency give more protection in female athletes (over 15 min, 2-3 times weekly), and ACL benefits held with under 20 minutes per week but were larger with 3+ sessions.
Warm-up injury prevention programmes in children and adolescents reduce injuries by about 36% overall, and compliance is the main source of variation.
FIFA 11+ reduces football injuries by about 39%, ankle injuries by about 32% and head and neck injuries by about 40%; the original FIFA 11 showed no effect.
FIFA 11+ Kids cut injuries by 57% in boys aged 7-13, with more sessions per week giving more benefit, but in real-world use coaches dropped the full programme because of time and motivation.
In schoolboy rugby (14-18 years), a movement-control warm-up reduced concussions, and teams doing it 3+ times weekly had 72% fewer match injuries.
findings.effect: Match injuries RR 0.28 in high-dose teams

findings.finding: Adherence drives results: players with high FIFA 11+ adherence had better balance and about 72% lower injury risk; coach workshops raised adherence more than an unsupervised website, and coaches and players rarely believed a warm-up prevented knee or ankle injuries.

Youth neuromuscular warm-ups also improve function: a basketball programme in 15-year-old boys reduced injuries and improved muscle reaction times; school-based NMT reduced injuries in middle and high school girls.
findings.dose: about 3 months to a full season

findings.finding: A physical literacy based neuromuscular warm-up for 8-12-year-olds was feasible and enjoyable and improved movement skill, jumps and sprint.
